title: The New Boy
part: PART TWO: THE TOLL OF ONE STORY

pages.text:
*From the Bridgewater Almanac: Newcomers are like weeds: give them a season and they will either take root or go away.*

Rue Alder had spent the last seven days with the friendliest person she had ever met. She had also spent the last seven days sitting at the end of the bench by the wall, eating her lunch alone.

It was a strange thing. You would think that having a secret friend would make the empty bench feel less empty. But it did the opposite. Now, when the other children laughed, Rue heard the echo of a different kind of laughter. She heard Hobb humming a tune that did not have a name, right inside her head. It made the real laughter in the yard feel very loud and very thin, like paper being torn.

She looked at the chestnut tree. Under it sat Perrin Fen. He was still wearing his wool hat, the one that was two sizes too big and looked as if it had swallowed him whole. He was drawing in a small notebook. His fingers were stained blue with ink, up to the second knuckle.

Rue stood up. She put her squashed cheese sandwich in her coat pocket. It was a brave thing to do. She felt her heart doing a small, nervous flip in her chest, the way a coin does when you drop it into a jar and it hits the bottom.

"Right then," she said to the air.
pages.image: A small freckled girl in a yellow raincoat stands in a schoolyard, looking across the grass toward a boy in an oversized hat sitting under a large tree.

pages.text:
Perrin did not look up; he was busy. His pencil moved in tiny, careful circles, sketching the texture of the bark, while Rue walked over and sat down on the grass. She left a polite distance of about two feet between them, which was close enough to be a friend but far enough to run away if necessary.

She said nothing.

For a very long time, the only sound was the scratch of his pencil and the distant chatter of the Bridge Club. Rue looked at the leaves, which were turning a color like dried apple juice, and she watched a beetle crawl along a root as she waited.

Perrin’s pencil stopped. He did not turn around, but his shoulders relaxed, just a little, because he was waiting, too. It was exactly right, and better than any conversation she had ever tried to start, because there was no need to fill the silence with the wrong words. They just sat there, two people who were good at being alone, making a kind of quiet company.
pages.image: Two children sitting on the grass under a chestnut tree, keeping a respectful distance, watching a beetle crawl on a root while autumn leaves fall around them.

pages.text:
Finally, Perrin closed his notebook. He held it out to her, not with a word, but with a steady hand. The cover was plain brown leather, worn smooth at the corners.

Rue opened it.

Her breath caught. Inside were drawings of the bridges. Not just sketches, but maps. Every stone was there. The cracks were marked with tiny, precise lines. There were four of them, each one detailed so carefully that she could almost feel the roughness of the granite.

But the last page was different. It was a drawing of the old bridge, but from underneath. The arch was shown from the water's perspective, looking up. The roots of the trees were tangled in the shadow. The stones were drawn with a softness that made them look like they were breathing.

"I couldn't see the bottom," Perrin said. His voice was quiet, barely louder than the wind. "I wanted to."
pages.image: A boy with ink-stained fingers holds a small leather notebook open to a detailed drawing of a bridge arch from below, showing intricate stone work and tree roots.

pages.text:
"Two weeds!"

The voice was sharp and thin, cutting through the morning air. Cedric Pettibone strode past, his red waistcoat standing out brightly against the dull grey coats of the Bridge Club, while Skye Tanner walked beside him, her long braid swinging like a pendulum.

She glanced at Rue, then looked down at her own boots, as if the patch of grass had suddenly grown a fascinating new pattern.

Rue felt the old sting of embarrassment prick at her skin, but it did not take hold. It slid right off her, just like water does off the hood of a raincoat. She looked at Perrin. He had not flinched, nor had he looked away, and he simply stood there with the quiet steadiness of a boy who has learned not to expect the world to look back.

"Thanks," he said. Just that. One word, soft and clear as a bell.

Rue smiled, and this time it was a real smile, not the practiced cheerful face she wore for teachers. "You're welcome," she said.

Perrin tucked the notebook into his pocket, his ink-stained fingers smearing slightly on the leather. "I haven't spoken to anyone since April," he said, "except a goat. But he didn't answer."
pages.image: A skinny boy in a red waistcoat sneers as he walks past, while a tall girl with a braid looks at the ground, and two children sit calmly on the grass under a tree.

pages.text:
That evening, Rue went under the arch. She carried Perrin’s notebook, which she had asked to borrow. Hobb was sitting on his favorite rock, his spectacles mended with twine, turning his head slowly to let the moss settle on his shoulders.

Rue sat down. She opened the notebook to the last page, the one of the arch.

"Hobb," she said. "There’s a boy. His name is Perrin. He draws bridges. He knows what the bottom looks like."

Hobb’s ears, which were shaped like leaves, perked up. He leaned forward, his breath smelling of tea and old books. He looked at the drawing, and then at Rue. He blinked, once, and then again, as if checking the ink had not run.

"You can't bring him," he said. His voice was high, almost a squeak. It was the voice of a man who was terrified and delighted in exactly the same amount.

Rue shook her head. "Not yet," she said. "I’m just telling you. So you know the town is watching."

Hobb let out a long, slow breath. The moss around his feet rippled out in a wide, gentle wave.
pages.image: A large mossy troll with round spectacles leans in to look at a small notebook held by a girl, his expression a mix of surprise and worry, while moss ripples around his feet.
